title: Your fridge doesn’t make cold, it pumps heat out
body: Cold is just a lack of heat, so a refrigerator works by moving heat from inside to the kitchen. A refrigerant flows around a sealed loop: it evaporates in pipes inside the fridge, soaking up heat as it turns to gas, then a compressor squeezes that gas until it is hot enough to shed the heat through coils on the back or sides. That is why those parts of a fridge feel warm.

slides.heading: The refrigerant’s journey, in order
slides.explanation: Liquid boils inside and soaks up heat; the compressor makes the gas hot enough to shed it outside, where it condenses; a valve then drops its pressure.

steps.label: Boils inside the fridge, soaking up heat
Compressed until hotter than the room
Condenses in outside coils, shedding heat
Expands through a valve; pressure drops

slides.heading: 1. Evaporate
slides.text: Low-pressure liquid refrigerant boils inside the fridge at well below freezing, absorbing heat from the food, much as evaporating sweat cools your skin.

slides.heading: 2. Compress
slides.text: A compressor squeezes the gas. Compression raises its temperature above the room’s, so heat can now flow out of it into the kitchen.

slides.heading: 3. Condense and expand
slides.text: In the outside coils the gas cools and turns back into liquid. It then passes through a narrow valve, its pressure drops, and the cycle starts again.

slides.heading: The twist
slides.text: Leaving the fridge door open warms your kitchen overall: the heat it removes is dumped back into the room, plus extra heat from the motor’s work.
